Business.title: From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
Business.text:
From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance, the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines.

The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves.

These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand.

So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean.

While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions.

This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers.

Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam".

Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets.

In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes.

In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump.

Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto.

Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name.

Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes.

The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy, external used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain.

ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies.

A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day.

While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges.

XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin.

The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation.

Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain.

This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value.

Business.title: Ofcom outlines age verification for under-16s ahead of social media ban
Business.text:
Ofcom has set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

Under the UK's social media ban - which is due to come into force in March next year - those under that age will be prevented from accessing ten of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

Many UK adults are also likely to have to confirm that they are not under-age by using one of the proposed measures, which are subject to government approval.

A similar ban was introduced in Australia last year but many children there have found ways to get round it. The UK says it intends to take a tougher approach.

Age verification below 18 is challenging because 16 and 17 year olds don't have credit cards or full driving licences, and may not have passports either. They can also look significantly older or younger than they are.

To address that challenge, Ofcom has - in addition to traditional forms of ID - recommended four methods that it says would be "highly effective" at gauging people's ages:

photo ID matching, where relevant information on a photo ID document such as a passport is checked against a live image taken during an age check

banking-based checks, which involves using the information a financial institution has on record regarding a user's age

face age estimation technology (which the regulator argues has recently improved)

digital ID services, which enable people to digitally prove who they are or provide information about themselves, such as their age

The BBC has asked three of the UK's biggest banks whether they would have a process for assisting with social media requests for age verification if it did become an official measure.

However, ultimately it will be up to the tech companies to figure out how to implement the checks: the onus is on social network providers to come up with their own solutions and comply.

Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes said the regulator was drawing on its experience in introducing tougher age checks for porn sites last year:

"What we've learned in introducing age checks across the porn industry is that actually what a lot of countries did before us was say you need to do it this way and they were very prescriptive and it didn't work," she told the BBC.

"So what we've said all along is here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you."

Some of the tech companies, including Meta, have called for age verification to be applied at device level, so that someone under-age would be automatically blocked from installing social media apps via app stores.

Meta told the BBC it already applies some methods recommended by Ofcom to enforce its user age requirements or place users in Teen Accounts settings.

But it said applying age checks at device-level, via app stores, could reduce the burden on people to have to repeatedly verify their age across multiple platforms.

This would place responsibility with Apple and Google, who between them operate most of the world's smartphones. Apple has already introduced age verification in the UK.

However Ofcom says that would not absolve the social network providers from doing their own checks as well.

The regulator said it didn't have a firm number for how many adults would need to prove they were not under age, but conceded that it would be a "large number of accounts" that social media companies would need to "deal with."

It has also acknowledged that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", and some children would succeed in bypassing the age checks.

Dawes said making the ban work would be a joint effort.

"At Ofcom, what we will do is make sure that the services that the social media companies put in the checks that they need to," she told BBC News.

"That's our job, but the wider question about how everybody engages with this, it is for everybody, really.

"I actually think the real prize here is going to be for today's eight to 10-year-olds entering secondary school without it being the norm to go on Snap in your class group chat, without it being the norm to have all your sports fixtures organised on Instagram."

Ofcom's age verification report will now be considered by the government, with a decision due by the end of the year.

Child safety campaigners including the Molly Rose Foundation and NSPCC welcomed Ofcom's guidance.

But both said there were lessons to be learned from how Australia's social media ban had been implemented, after it was found many under-16s could still access social platforms.

"That's why, as we prepare to embark on our own social media ban in the UK, we need to make sure we accurately know the age of child users," said Rani Govender, head of child safety online at the NSPCC.

She said the government and Ofcom must ensure tech firms are held accountable for meeting age check standards "to help keep children safe online and ensure the ban delivers change in practice".

But Andy Burrows, the Molly Rose Foundation's chief executive, said Ofcom had shown a "dire track record" of enforcing the Online Safety Act - raising questions over how effectively it would help deliver a social media ban.

"Andy Burnham must deliver a ban that learns the lessons from Australia and that incentivises safety-by-design as the price of admission to the UK market, with a ban as the starting point in a proper plan to give children a safe and happy online life," he said.

Jonny Blunt, corporate affairs director of BT's consumer division, said families should "prepare children for life online after the ban and highlight the risks of trying to dodge the restrictions".

"Having those conversations now and giving young people time to prepare for the changes in March will be crucial in helping them adapt to a significant change for a whole generation," he said.

"The restrictions have the potential to change the way young people interact with the digital world for the better, but only if regulators, tech companies, families, and educators come together to make it a success."

Additional reporting by Liv McMahon and Chris Vallance

Business.title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’
Business.text:
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.

Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.

Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars.

Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.

TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack.

Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.

Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets.

The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who was jailed for four months in 2024 after pleading guilty to money laundering violations. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.

In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.”

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.

North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.

Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service.

Tether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m. The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers.

Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.

Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.

The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

A spokesperson for the FCA said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.”

The Bank of England is also monitoring the hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment.

Coinbase, another major cryptocurrency exchange, said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.

In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

Sports.title: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure
Sports.text:
When Sir Jim Ratcliffe became a co-owner of Manchester United in 2024, much of the narrative centred on his desire to rebuild the club around a British core.

Given the expense of buying homegrown players, and the difficulties Michael Carrick - the first permanent British managerial appointment of the Ineos era - has faced this season, perhaps Ratcliffe is rethinking.

But if Carrick fails to stop the rot and loses his job, United are already considering the merits of appointing another British coach - albeit one who is more experienced.

That Eddie Howe is a contender for a job that remains one of the most high-profile in world football isn't hard to fathom.

Speak to those who have worked alongside Howe and they describe a man whose track record of improving players is a direct result of his relentless approach on the training field.

They will also tell you Howe is someone who places an unwavering importance on the methodology of setting a winning culture.

Howe may lack experience at one of the traditional top-six clubs, but his body of work at Bournemouth and Newcastle is impressive.

Having been appointed Bournemouth boss with the club facing relegation from League Two in January 2009, Howe led them to the Premier League in 2015. He went on to establish the Cherries as a top-flight club before leaving - for a second time - in 2020.

In 2021, Howe was appointed Newcastle manager. He led them from relegation trouble to qualification for the Champions League on two occasions and won the EFL Cup - the club's first trophy in 56 years - in 2025.

Of course, managing Manchester United is an altogether different proposition.

Indeed, Howe's emergence as a potential successor to Carrick has been greeted with negativity in some circles.

Sections of the fanbase have been vocal on social media with their opinion that Howe isn't a big enough name to replace Carrick.

Former United players Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt also fell short of providing their backing to Howe on their podcast, though it is worth pointing out they spoke in favour of the 48-year-old's potential appointment when Ruben Amorim was sacked in January.

Ex-captain Roy Keane is among those to have backed Howe as a possible successor to Carrick, and other former top-flight players - including Darren Bent, Gareth Barry and Jack Wilshere - have also touted him as the man for the job.

Of course, if you look hard enough you'll find voices for and against every potential manager, and it will be up to United chief executive Omar Berrada, sporting director Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell to weigh up how they proceed.

Their first decision will be what happens with Carrick, and Saturday's match against Chelsea is likely to have a bearing on how United move forward.

If Carrick does depart, finances will inevitably be a factor.

The former Middlesbrough boss and his staff will need to be paid up before United even get to factoring in the monetary commitment towards their next head coach.

While the details of Howe's agreement with Newcastle when he left in the summer remain confidential, it is understood that as things stand any club or national team would be required to pay a seven-figure compensation fee to the Magpies.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle - with a view to protecting themselves against Howe walking straight into another club - reached an agreement over a compensation structure that decreases over time.

It is understood that figure started at £6m but has already reduced by half.

The compensation payments have an expiry date - understood to be before the end of the season - at which point he can be appointed for nothing.

Of course, in an industry in which astronomical figures are the norm, the prospect of paying a maximum of £3m for Howe may not be too problematic.

That said, given the amount Manchester United have spent on hiring and firing managers in recent years, it is understandable if Berrada and Wilcox want to keep costs down.

Howe is an obvious contender for the Manchester United job, just as he would be if the England head coach's position became available.

Whether he is offered it or not will give a clear indication about the path United are going down.

Director of football Jason Wilcox is thought to favour the 48-year-old, with director of recruitment Christopher Vivell preferring former Bayern Munich and Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann.

Ultimately, their recommendations will be assessed by chief executive Omar Berrada, with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairs Joel and Avram Glazer having the final say.

It is not completely clear where the negativity about Howe moving to Old Trafford comes from, other than Wilcox being targeted by Manchester United fans during the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth.

In the current managerial climate, few managers get the chance to build a body at work at one club over a number of years as, for instance, Sir Alex Ferguson did at Aberdeen before he moved south in November 1986.

There is clearly a general disillusionment among the club's matchgoing fans around the football decisions taken since Ratcliffe bought his minority stake in early 2024, but Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have all been backed.

Some say no manager can succeed at United with the structure as it is, and it is clear whoever is in charge needs to mould together a squad bought by six permanent managers, most of whom have differing playing styles.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta warns Max Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' after red card against Fleetwood
Sports.text:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has told Max Dowman "we are not in Disneyland" and that he intends to hold the teenager to the same standards as other first-team players.

Dowman, 16, was sent off in the 85th minute of Arsenal's penalty shoot-out loss to Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday after reacting to a heavy challenge by Harrison Neal and will serve a three-match ban.

A visibly annoyed Arteta spoke to Dowman as the teenager left the pitch, and on Friday spoke about the incident for the first time, saying he warned the attacker before the game about dealing with provocation.

"I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction, whether it is positive or negative. But you need to understand the context and the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out," Arteta said of his words to Dowman.

"But, I don't know. You can have another reaction. If you see the reaction of my father and my mother with me some days you might say 'I don't like the reaction'. For me, it was the best reaction to be who I am."

Arteta revealed that he had spoken to Dowman on Thursday and said there were "no issues at all" between the pair. However, he added that he needs to be "very straight" with Dowman and clear of the standards expected.

Dowman was sent off for the England U19s earlier this month where he was also on the end of heavy challenges in a match with the United States.

Of that red card, Arteta said: "They are his age. They are 16 – the same. What is the reaction? That is the level and that is the reaction.

"And whether it is right or wrong, that is the reaction."

Arteta also spoke of the impact the red card had on the team, saying: "And the reaction when I don't win, you want to know what my reaction is? I am [angry] big time.

"So, we need to be ready for that. This is the environment and this is the reality, otherwise we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League and this level.

"We look after him so much that you cannot imagine.

"But at the same time we are going to demand from him, like everybody else, because he needs to earn the right to play. Because the other boys, what are they going to tell me? You need to be fair."

The Gunners did appeal against the red card but the Football Association (FA) upheld the decision. Of that, Arteta said he was "very disappointed", adding "we are lucky today that he (Dowman) hasn't had a broken foot."

Sports.title: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts set up epic finale - what do stats and history suggest could happen?
Sports.text:
Third Test, Cape Town (day four of five)

South Africa 329 & 387: Mulder 115, Rickelton 101

Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104

Australia need 288 to win

A gripping series has the finale it deserves.

Having effectively began day four on 40-4, South Africa batted on and on against Australia in Cape Town to move from a position where defeat looked likely to one where a series victory is a real possibility.

In being bowled out for 387 in the final over - with Ryan Rickelton making 101 and Wiaan Mulder last man out for a brilliant 115 - South Africa set the tourists a target of 288 for victory.

WinViz - the tool analysts CricViz use to predict such results - gives the hosts a 54% chance of victory.

If only things were that simple…

Australia's target is such that should they chase it on day five, it would be the second-highest fourth-innings chase in the 62 previous Tests on this famous ground.

The highest? That's a good omen for Australia.

They chased 331 for a four-wicket win in an epic Test against the Proteas in 2002, when Ricky Ponting hit a brilliant 100 not out.

There have been five other scores above 288 in the fourth innings at Newlands - all of which were made in defeats or when salvaging a draw.

For much of the afternoon and evening sessions, as Australia's bowlers tired, this surface appeared flat enough to score.

When Rickelton and Mulder applied themselves, few opportunities were created. They were able to progress to their third and fourth Test centuries respectively.

It took a run out to end Rickelton's knock, after which Marco Jansen pulled to deep square leg and Gerald Coetzee was also run out - three dismissals down to batter error in a collapse of 4-61, which left South Africa nine down and 251 runs ahead.

That Mulder and number 11 Kagiso Rabada flogged 36 before the close, suggested run-scoring is not impossible.

None of those late runs were made under the pressure of a chase, however.

The wicket of Simon Harmer in the final session, bowled shouldering arms by a ball from Nathan Lyon which turned back sharply showed the difficulty ahead.

Harmer dismissed Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey in Australia's first innings - all recognised batters.

The 37-year-old Essex legend, who once considered playing for England, will be crucial.

As ever in such scenarios, the pitch will play its part.

The PitchViz rating - CricViz's way of assessing the difficulty of a surface - jumped to 6.6 in the final session, comfortably the highest (thus most difficult) rating of the Test.

After settling down in the morning, the ball, as would be expected as a Test progresses, was turning significantly more in the final session than at any point across the previous four days.

Interestingly, however, South Africa's false shot percentage was just 11% across day four, a drop from 18% on day three.

Uneven bounce has not yet been a factor but one ball to Rickelton shortly after tea also shot low.

Sports.title: Ellie Kildunne: how Red Roses star ended up benched by England
Sports.text:
She's the poster girl. She's the former World Player of the Year. She came second at BBC Sports Personality of the Year. She lit up the 2025 Rugby World Cup. She's even got her own Barbie doll.

So why isn't Ellie Kildunne starting for England against the USA on Friday night (21:15 kick-off)?

First of all she is human, let's not forget that.

We're all allowed ups and downs. It's just that Kildunne's dip comes with the large spotlight of her being the Red Roses' household name.

None of her team-mates come close to her popularity with fans both in and outside rugby union with her 239,000 Instagram followers. Her face and name are used for clicks by all the media, present company included.

However, if you follow the sport and watch her play, no-one is undroppable.

England suffered their first loss in four years to end their 41-Test unbeaten streak in Toronto against Canada. In that fixture and their previous match with the same opposition in Exeter, Kildunne, 27, was a target for the opposition. She was never given space, defenders stepped up, her arms were pulled and balls were spilt.

When England head coach John Mitchell benched her after England's loss in Toronto he was clear that "it isn't disputed that she adds huge value".

However, he went on to add: "She's just going through a difficult period at the moment, and it's important for us to help her through that.

"She wants to become consistent as well, and she'll get back. It's also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you're competing in the Red Roses.

"So it's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game, and that goes for everyone."

The key word we can take from that is "consistent" - mainly because Mitchell said it twice.

Kildunne remains one of the world's most phenomenal players when it comes to gainline success and metres gained.

Much of this is due to poor opposition defence, but her statistics show a decline over the past three seasons at international level.

It seems almost harsh to highlight as these are numbers other players could only dream of but she's also gone from beating an average of six defenders a game in 2024, to 4.2 in 2026.

Kildunne has also conceded more penalties in 2026 than either of the previous two years. Some of these statistics, althought not all, are mirrored in her PWR performances last season.

While Canada are not alone, it does appear they are one of the best teams at dealing with Kildunne's threats.

In their drawn match in Exeter, Kildunne made 17 carries for 47 metres, an average of 2.8m, which is well below her usual standards. In Toronto she had the ball turned over twice - that was her joint-most in any England game.

Emma Sing now appears to have some purchase on the England 15 shirt and it is well deserved. She is a different full-back to Kildunne, which is a bonus for the Red Roses.

Sing has three PWR titles with her club side Gloucester-Hartpury and has been one of their most reliable players throughout that period. She has got a monster boot round the park and off the tee and, while Sing might not score the same worldies we have seen from Kildunne, her highlights reel is none too shabby.

On Sing's starting selection in Ottawa, Mitchell was happy to explain the players' differences: "They play quite differently. So we're very fortunate to have two very good full-backs. But you know, Emma's been sitting in the in the wings in this particular phase of our campaign.

"She was intermittent through injury for a long period of time. So she's in a really good physical place, and she's worked really, really hard. So I think it's time to give her an opportunity."

Sports.title: Jack Grealish dropped by Everton: The future for ex-England winger
Sports.text:
When Jack Grealish breezed back into Everton in his white Lamborghini one hour before the end of this summer's transfer deadline, the excitement among supporters and the player himself was clearly evident.

Grealish's previous spell on loan from Manchester City had been cut short by a serious foot injury, but the 31-year-old had produced enough moments of excitement to make his return to the Finch Farm training base a rare moment of joy amid a miserable summer in the transfer market.

When Grealish finally left in the early hours - with the deal done, every autograph signed and every selfie posed for - it was a sort of homecoming for an everyman personality Everton fans had come to regard as one of their own.

This was a move with a lot riding on it - for Everton manager David Moyes, who had been left with only 18 senior players after a botched transfer window, and especially for Grealish, whose exile from City at the start of the final year of his contract confirmed his banishment.

Now, Grealish's future and Everton's faith in him, has reached a defining moment.

Grealish's exclusion from Everton's squad before the Carabao Cup tie at home to Newcastle was publicly described as "a breach of club discipline".

Specifically, it was a failure to turn up for training on Monday, leaving the talented maverick - who was Britain's first £100m footballer when he signed for City from Aston Villa in summer 2021 - facing another rebuild in his career.

Everton's decision to go public before the game with the reasons for Grealish's absence emphasised the seriousness of his transgression.

The fall-out means this now looks increasingly like Grealish's 'now or never' moment, because failure at Everton will surely mark a downward spiral from the top echelons of the Premier League.

Everton do not regard this week's misdemeanour as marking the proverbial 'Last Chance Saloon' for Grealish. Moyes does not have enough players at his disposal to make rapid outcasts of potential game-changers.

But it increases the pressure on the former England forward to win back the faith of fans who love his obvious enjoyment of life and the magic he has shown he can produce.

Moyes will hope it is a harsh lesson learned, because Everton now have even more to play for, given Wembley has suddenly come into view in the Carabao Cup.

BBC Sport believes there have been occasional time-keeping issues with Grealish in the past, but nothing on this scale from a personality regarded as a hard trainer who, in general, keeps himself in good condition.

Grealish has held talks with those in authority at Everton, where it is sure to have been made crystal clear there must be no repeat, certainly not under a strict disciplinarian such as Moyes, and he must now attempt to be rehabilitated back into the squad.

The inevitable decision to punish Grealish, taken at a high level within the club but with input and full support from Moyes, leaves him at the crossroads.

That is especially the case because Everton gave arguably their best performance of the season to beat Newcastle United 3-1 and set up a quarter-final at League Two Fleetwood Town, conquerors of Premier League champions Arsenal in the last round.

And it was done with the more dynamic style of 20-year-old Tyrique George playing on the left flank, which Grealish might have been expected to occupy.

Moyes was guarded after the game and instead preferred to focus on a vital victory.

"You probably know I'm not going to give any details. It's a club decision and I support it. It's something I don't want to speak too much about," he said.

"The one thing about Everton is that they have got real good values. All the players stand behind it and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch, and I think the players did a good job.

"It is a small squad, but we are doing our best to keep challenging. We are not accepting any excuses for anything and I think the players are doing a great job. There was a humility about us."

The words were not specifically aimed at Grealish, but they might as well have been from a manager who will have been bitterly disappointed and angry about his transgression.

Moyes and Grealish formed a close relationship from virtually their first moment of contact in August 2025, the latter saying: "As soon as I spoke to the manager, I knew there was only one place that I wanted to go and that was Everton."

And Grealish, a key figure when Manchester City won the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023, played his part until sustaining a foot fracture that ended his season in Everton's 1-0 win at his former club Aston Villa in January.

Grealish's happiness with life at Everton was illustrated when he decided against returning to City, continuing his rehabilitation at Finch Farm rather than going back to Etihad Stadium.

Everton weighed up a second loan deal to bring Grealish back carefully, with his injury, finances and - to a certain extent - his character all entering the equation before Moyes decided to move again for a player who insisted Merseyside was the only place he wanted to be.

Moyes was also juggling very limited options as owners The Friedkin Group appeared to back away from serious squad strengthening as they prepared to put the club up for sale.

Grealish's form this season has been underwhelming, failing to score or create an assist in eight appearances - two of those at City before returning to Everton - while his tendency to slow play down is at odds with the usual tempo Moyes requires from his team.

Moyes' fury will have increased because Grealish, who missed Saturday's loss at Arsenal through "illness", is part of a paper-thin squad that simply cannot carry passengers or have players ruling themselves out through needless ill-discipline.

There will be frustration too, as Grealish is a hugely popular within Everton's dressing room as well as with staff in every area of the club. He has been described as "a lad with a heart of gold, kind and charming, who actually loves being here".

This was illustrated when he recently made a £10,000 donation to a GoFundMe page for Everton fan Leon Skapars, 36, a father of three who has been diagnosed with cancer.

The family are raising money in a search for treatment options, and Skapars' wife Crystal said: "In that moment, Jack gave our whole family something we desperately needed, hope. What he has done for our family is something we will never forget. It makes us feel incredibly emotional."

Grealish also appeared to present awards at the Daily Mirror's 'Pride Of Britain' event recently, saying: "Footballers are classed as heroes - but these are the real heroes."

On Friday, Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca refused to discuss Grealish's actions at Everton, but did praise his character.

Maresca said: "It's not correct to talk about Jack in this moment, first of all because he is an Everton player and secondly because I don't have all the information.

"I still think he is a good guy and has a big heart."

In April, Grealish extended his role as principal ambassador to Special Olympics Great Britain for a further three years, having first joined in 2022.

Grealish marked the occasion by hosting five of the 10 Special Olympics GB athletes who completed the London Marathon at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, surprising the athletes with a VIP experience, a stadium tour and spending time with them pitchside.

Those at Everton also regard Grealish as one of the first to engage with their community programme at Finch Farm, as well as meeting with the Everton in the Community Down Syndrome team.

Grealish often talks about the inspiration he takes from his sister Hollie, who has cerebral palsy.

He has, however, hit the headlines in less welcome circumstances over the years, and this latest incident ushered in more.

In April, Grealish was pictured asleep at a Manchester rooftop bar surrounded by drinks. It was a scene that is certainly not against the law but was at best unwise, especially with ever-present phone cameras around and the fact he was in rehabilitation from injury.

In March 2020, he was fined by his club Aston Villa and apologised publicly after breaking lockdown guidelines during the pandemic after leaving his house to visit a friend.

In November 2020, he admitted two counts of careless driving relating to two incidents in which a Citroen van and a Mercedes were damaged.

And yet, speak to most people in football - certainly at Everton - and the character references are unfailingly glowing about his outgoing personality and kind-hearted gestures, making his breach of discipline even more painful for his many admirers.

But after this latest setback, Grealish is running out of time and opportunities to justify that continued support.

Sports.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Set up to fail? Where England's World Cup campaign went wrong
Sports.text:
As Mikey Lewis darted over for a late try in a desperate - and almost certainly fruitless - points chase against Papua New Guinea, the obituaries were already being written for England's Men's Rugby League World Cup campaign.

Much earlier on Friday, England's women had lacked the power and nous to overcome Samoa, losing 24-6 in a match that decided who went through to the semi-finals.

England's men actually won their game - 34-12 - but it was nowhere near the margin of victory required. Their elimination will be confirmed on Sunday unless Tonga beat Samoa by more than 46 points.

And so the likelihood is that for the first time in World Cup history, neither England's men nor their women will feature in the last four.

For the men, that ends a run that began with Great Britain at the first tournament in 1954.

The disappointment will only reinforce the idea that English rugby league needs a serious period of introspection - as well as significant investment to keep pace with the game in the southern hemisphere.

But there have been other factors to trouble England at this World Cup, hosted by Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea at short notice after France pulled out for financial reasons.

Even before a ball was kicked, the men were faced with a sense of impending doom - brought on by injuries, shambolic travel arrangements and a bizarre format that had England facing immediate jeopardy with a testing opener against Tonga.

The northern hemisphere game has deep-rooted problems, and seems to be stuck in stasis when compared with the thriving NRL.

England had a record of being a major player at World Cups - having reached two finals and a further four semi-finals at the past six tournaments.

But when last autumn's 3-0 Ashes series defeat by Australia prompted the departure of head coach Shaun Wane, his successor was handed a near-impossible task.

Brian McDermott was appointed in April. Given just six months to prepare, the former Leeds Rhinos head coach had no mid-season international to work on a plan. Based in Australia because of his role as Gold Coast Titans assistant coach, he relied on virtual meetings to connect with his prospective squad and staff.

Four on-field sessions were planned in Australia before the World Cup. But only two were completed in full after his UK-based players were subjected to a 48-hour journey to Perth that left them exhausted - a situation McDermott compared to Planes, Trains and Automobiles, the 1987 road-trip comedy starring Steve Martin and John Candy.

It was a shambolic way to prepare for a pivotal opener against Tonga - one that always had the potential to consign the defeated team to an early elimination.

Following that 30-12 loss, McDermott said: "You give me another two or three weeks preparation or another couple of games of preparation leading into the tournament and I'd be really excited."

With the tournament organisers planning travel itineraries for the teams involved, any post-World Cup debrief ought to examine how that situation was allowed to occur.

It would have made more sense for England's opener to be against France - the only other team in the men's tournament made up largely of northern hemisphere-based players.

Wakefield Trinity's historic triumph may have delivered a wonderful sign-off story to the Super League season but it delivered another conundrum around England's squad selection.

Had McDermott known prior to 5 October that none of the Wakefield players in his thinking would be available, could arrangements have been made for his UK-based players to travel to Australia earlier?

In the end, only three of the 14 England-based players in the squad (George Williams, Matty Ashton and Ben Currie) participated in the Super League Grand Final on 3 October.

"If we come together next year as a group, we will be further down the track and we don't need to start from scratch," McDermott added.

"Bear in mind when we landed in Perth on the Friday [9 October], we are starting... like we didn't know each other.

"We were putting things in place about who we are as a group, what it means to us, how we are going to play, how we are going to attack and how we are going to defend. There's been a ton of work gone on."

While much of the pre-tournament noise centred on the omission of Jake Connor and England's long-running halves debate, very little focus was given to a decimated forward pack and other notable absentees.

Prior the first match, McDermott recounted Australia prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui's admiration for the strength of the English pack during last year's Ashes series.

England's ability to front up had also previously been talked up by Kangaroos boss Kevin Walters.

Yet McDermott had few of those same players at his disposal.

Matty Lees' season-ending injury in May was not only a blow for St Helens but also robbed England of a key enforcer, one who had previously shown he could stand up to the physicality of a powerhouse Tonga front row.

With second-rower Mike McMeeken and prop Caleb Hamlin-Uele unavailable, Morgan Smithies withdrawing from the squad injured and a calf complaint taking Morgan Knowles out of the equation for the encounter against Tonga, England were left short in that area.

That is before you even get to options such as Sydney Roosters' Billy Smith, Wigan's Jake Wardle and Leeds Rhinos duo Ash Handley and Mikolaj Oledzki, all absent through injury.

And when England had to chase the scoreboard after their defeat by Tonga - while hoping results elsewhere went in their favour - it left them in trouble.

They failed to get the numbers on the board they needed against Papua New Guinea. McDermott acknowledged that it left him and his players waiting for the inevitable.

"It feels like we lost the game," he said. "We won and, in any circumstances I would be really proud but I think something remarkable is going to have to happen now for us to go through.

"We've made massive strides together in such a short period of time, in difficult circumstances where the narrative of the last two weeks is that you've got to win by 70 and 60. You don't just need to win, you need to win by massive margins."

Whenever the Women's Rugby League World Cup has featured semi-finals previously, England or Great Britain have always been there. When it has not, they have always finished in the top four.

But this time, they approached the tournament with a different focus, as head coach Staurt Barrow opted for youth over experience.

His squad contained 11 players aged 23 or under, and was largely comprised of players who have full-time occupations away from rugby league.

And that told as England were humbled 78-0 by world champions Australia last Saturday, and found wanting by a Samoa side dominated by NRL Women's Premiership talent. While Australia's domestic league pays its players, money is much tighter in England's Women's Super League.

"Women's Super League has progressed to a certain level and we are bringing young players through so that creeps into the national team," said Barrow.

"It's good and refreshing - but at the same rate we are progressing, it's probably accelerating quicker on this side of the world if I am really honest.

"The investment into the NRLW is not only making the Jillaroos better but it's making all the Pacific nations better as well.

"I think nearly every player for Samoa has played NRLW at some stage and that competition is improving at a rate of knots. We'll have to go back and look at what we can do in our competition.

"We definitely need to do something because the acceleration of the game over here is phenomenal at the moment.

"Back home, we need to have more investment into the women's and girls game. It can't just be a token gesture at some clubs - and I'm not saying it is, but we need to put money into it."

Barrow's other main problem relates to geography and an international calendar that leaves them ill-prepared to face the leading southern hemisphere nations.

Aside from a record 90-4 defeat by Australia in Las Vegas, England's women have been limited to six international fixtures since the previous World Cup, all against France and Wales - in which they have scored 348 points, while conceding four.

"We lost to the better side on the day. I am not going to deny that," Barrow added.

"It was a good game and a good game for England to be in because we have a problem at the moment where we play France or Wales. And no disrespect to those nations but we win them [games] - and we play the Jillaroos and lose heavily.

"This was a nice game to be in where it was competitive all the way. The more of those we can get will definitely help us as a nation."

Sports.title: Lewis Hamilton says F1 has 'never had anyone like me' as Ferrari driver vows before Mexico Grand Prix to keep racing until sport returns to Africa
Sports.text:
Lewis Hamilton says he is unlike any driver Formula 1 has seen before and reaffirmed a determination to keep racing into his mid-forties.

The seven-time world champion recently said he wanted to continue in the sport to fulfil a dream of racing in Africa, having campaigned for a Grand Prix there for many years.

F1 has signed a 10-year deal with the central-east African country of Rwanda starting in the early 2030s which will be a first race on the continent since 1993.

The Briton said F1 had "never had anyone like me in the 70 years" of the sport and he felt like he was "built differently".

Hamilton will be at least 45 when that race takes place - the same age as Aston Martin driver Fernando Alonso, who is continuing in F1 next year - but he told a news conference before this weekend's Mexico Grand Prix that he should be considered a special case.

"Of course there are challenges up ahead that I can't foresee that come with age. But along this journey there have been so many pre-conceived ideas like that your reaction time drops off," he said.

"Did you see my reaction time in the last race? It was faster than some of the youngest people here.

"As long as you are willing to sacrifice everything, which I am right now – I can't say in four years whether I will want to continue doing what I'm doing – but I am still all in. I will be for the foreseeable future."

Sports.title: Premier League predictions: Chris Sutton v Bad Day At The Office star John Hannah - & AI
Sports.text:
Premier League champions Arsenal endured one of the most embarrassing nights in their history when they were knocked out of the Carabao Cup by League Two side Fleetwood Town on Tuesday, but can they bounce back at Anfield on Sunday?

"Arsenal put a pretty strong team out but were humiliated by Fleetwood, and at Highbury too," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Liverpool seem to be getting it together so this will be a big test for Mikel Arteta's side after the week they have had."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week eight, he takes on actor John Hannah, star of new action thriller Bad Day At The Office, who is an Arsenal fan.

Bad Day At The Office will be in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 October.

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Hannah, also known for his roles in Four Weddings and a Funeral, Sliding Doors and The Mummy, has been an Arsenal fan since he moved to London from Scotland more than 40 years ago.

As a boy growing up in East Kilbride he had hopes of becoming a footballer long before realising his acting aspirations.

Many of his childhood friends, including Rangers legend Ally McCoist, would go on to forge professional careers.

"I'd like to compare myself to Bukayo Saka," Hannah explained when describing what kind of player he was. "I played on the right wing and I was quite small and fast and I scored a lot of of goals.

"My dream was to be a footballer, and it was all I ever thought about. I played or trained all the time - but, like many dreams, it didn't come true.

"As I got a bit bigger I kind of segued back into midfield but when I discovered women and beer then I kind of stopped playing.

"Once I went to drama school I got very focused on that and then with moving to London and working away, around probably 20 years passed without me kicking a ball.

"But then in 2013 I did a film called Shooting for Socrates, where I played Northern Ireland manager Billy Bingham at the 1986 World Cup.

"We were down in Spain doing some filming there and had a bit of a kickaround and I remember thinking 'yeah, I've still got it you know!'

"Not anymore though - since then I have snapped my ACL [anterior cruciate ligament] which has put paid to football and a lot of sport. It is really just cycling and running for me now."

Chris Sutton and John Hannah were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Stamford Bridge, 12:30 GMT

Everyone will be watching this game because of Michael Carrick's situation at Manchester United, and wondering how much longer he will be in charge.

Carrick kept his job after the heavy defeats against Como and Bournemouth last week and my view is that, by keeping him on for now, they are possibly just prolonging the misery for him, really.

Going by how insipid United were against Bournemouth, it is hard to see them going to Chelsea and getting anything.

Chelsea were not much better in their defeat by Tottenham last weekend and since then they have been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Liverpool too.

Xabi Alonso is still without the injured Joao Pedro so I expect Danny Welbeck will lead their attack like he did against Liverpool, and Cole Palmer will be back after his suspension.

Chelsea have had a bad week but I can't see things changing for United, even if Bruno Fernandes is back in their team.

Sutton's prediction: 3-1

Sports.title: Maxence Lacroix could be out until January for Chelsea
Sports.text:
Chelsea fear defender Maxence Lacroix is set for a lengthy lay-off after suffering a serious hamstring injury.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that the France international, 26, could be out until January, meaning he could miss up to 10 matches.

The setback occurred at the end of the first half of Wednesday's Carabao Cup loss to Liverpool on penalties, as Lacroix sprinted and attempted to block a shot.

Sources inside Chelsea, including manager Xabi Alonso, have been guarded on the length of the absence.

When asked about Lacroix's injury at his media conference before Saturday's Premier League visit of Manchester United, Alonso said: "Max, he picked up an injury, and we expect that he's not going to be ready before the international break. So he will be a few weeks out."

The injury is a blow for Alonso, who has started his £52m summer signing from Crystal Palace in all but one of Chelsea's 11 matches across all competitions this season.

Only attacker Morgan Rogers has played more than Lacroix for Chelsea this season.

The Blues have a six-man centre-back group featuring Levi Colwill, Wesley Fofana, Josh Acheampong, Jorrel Hato and Aaron Anselmino as alternatives, although the latter two are also currently injured, with others having also lined up at full-back.

Asked about the potential replacements, Alonso added: "With Max's injury, we have Wes, we have Levi [Colwill], Josh [Acheampong], he could play as well as centre-back.

"Jorrel when he is back with the team [is an option]. Wes has played [and] even if he missed the penalty [in the shootout], I think that he had a good game.

"He was consistent, he was strong and I saw many positives from his performance. We know the level that he has had and he's going to be important."

Alonso also revealed that goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez is having a special mask fitted to play while recovering from a broken jaw and midfielder Moises Caicedo avoided injury despite concerns after the midweek clash with Liverpool.

Sports.title: Guangzhou Open: Harriet Dart reaches second WTA Tour semi-final of career
Sports.text:
Britain's Harriet Dart reached the second WTA Tour semi-final of her career when she fought back from a set down to beat fifth seed Paula Badosa at the Guangzhou Open in China.

The 30-year-old triumphed 3-6 6-2 6-4 against Spain's Badosa - ranked 54 places above her - in two hours and 15 minutes at Nansha International Tennis Centre.

Dart's first appearance in the semi-finals of a tour event was in the Transylvania Open in Cluj-Napoca, where she lost in straight sets to Karolina Pliskova.

She will face 16-year-old Chinese wildcard Sun Xinran in the last four on Saturday.

"It's been a very long time since I've been in the business end of the tournament so I am really excited for that," Dart said.

"Tennis is so stressful, so to have the opportunity to compete again on Saturday is a great opportunity for me."

Dart, who came through qualifying and beat second-seed Janice Tjen in the previous round, lost her opening service game in the first set but broke back and drew level at 3-3.

However, former world number two Badosa broke Dart's serve again to take a 5-3 lead and held her serve to close out the set.

The pair exchanged breaks at the start of the second set before Dart seized the upper hand to level at 1-1.

Badosa, who required two medical timeouts during the match as she appeared to struggle with the heat, saved a match point at 5-3 in the deciding set and then broke Dart's serve.

But the Spaniard, ranked 61st in the world, was running on empty in her next service game, as Dart won it to love.

"It was an incredible battle. I thought Paula started really strongly. I was always behind, and knew it was going to be an incredibly tough match," Dart added.

"I really needed to hang in there during the tough moments and wait for a chance. Luckily I was able to take my chance, and I am very excited to be in the semi-finals."

Sports.title: Packers beat Panthers as Green Bay’s Christian Watson returns after mid-game hospital visit
Sports.text:
Jordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to beat the Carolina Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night.

Love went 30 of 41 for 288 yards with touchdown passes to Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Jacobs plus an interception. Although he rushed for only 39 yards on 21 carries against the NFL’s lowest-ranked run defense, Jacobs scored on a four-yard catch and one-yard run for the Packers (5-3).

After trailing 27-10 in the third quarter, Carolina cut Green Bay’s lead to 27-19 on Bryce Young’s 26-yard touchdown pass to Jalen Coker on a fourth-and-three play with 5:37 remaining. Young’s ensuing two-point conversion pass was incomplete.

The Panthers (3-4) got the ball back at their own 45 before losing the ball on downs at midfield with 2:41 remaining. Carolina got one last chance from their own 20 with 22 seconds and no timeouts remaining, but Dani Dennis-Sutton’s sack essentially ended any comeback hopes.

Young went 23 of 31 for 209 yards with one touchdown and one interception. Carolina’s Chuba Hubbard had 22 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown and seven catches for 38 yards.

Green Bay’s Christian Watson was involved in a remarkable sequence of events. He hurt his chest making a 53-yard catch in the second quarter. The Packers feared he may have sustained a serious injury, and he was taken to a local hospital. However, after being passed fit by doctors, he returned late in ​the ​third quarter, then caught ​a six-yard pass on the ​opening play of ‌the fourth. He finished as the game’s top receiver with 113 yards on eight receptions.

“I never wanted to go [to hospital], I was hoping they’d let me off,” Watson said after the game. “They said there were a couple of signs that made them want to take me over there, so I was just praying it was good enough that I could come back out here. Luckily it was … I’m happy to be out here on a football field. There was no internal bleeding [nothing] that was raising suspicion. I cleared everything and I was able to get back out.”

Watson said he had been able to follow the game while he was in hospital. “One of the doctors had his phone out, so I was watching the play-by-play,” he said.

Carolina cornerback Will Lee hurt his hamstring while diving to make a tackle on the same play in which Watson was injured, and he was carted into the locker room. Carolina already have three other cornerbacks on injured reserve: Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), Mike Jackson (groin) and Jaycee Horn (quadriceps).

Brewers get big welcome

There was a warm welcome for another Wisconsin team on Thursday night. Several members of the Milwaukee Brewers, including team captain Christian Yelich and Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski, received a huge ovation as they arrived Lambeau Field one night after winning the first World Series title in franchise history.

Brewers pitcher Brandon Woodruff held the Commissioner’s Trophy aloft as he emerged from the tunnel during a timeout before the second quarter. A few of the players attempted a Lambeau Leap into the crowd, with outfielder Sal Frelick having the most success.

Those Brewers players later were shown on the video board cheering as they wore cheeseheads that included the message, “2026 WS Champions.”

Gaming_Tech.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
Gaming_Tech.text:
US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.

Shares in Intel continued their overnight slide into early trading on Friday, falling as much as 30% after the chip maker warned of a weaker computer market even as it plans to increase spending on AI.

Amazon shares fell as far as 6% before recovering after its reported earnings on Thursday evening fell short of investors' expectations.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange opened on Friday at its lowest level in more than two months, down 2.5%, as other tech stocks including Reddit and Roblox continued to fall.

The losses follow the value of Google owner Alphabet plunging by more than $500bn on Thursday after it revealed its own AI summaries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.

Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 1% after Thursday's massive slide.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value after its earnings update rattled investors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year, and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

Amazon on Thursday revealed the company was also spending more cash that it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.

Shares in Amazon recovered slightly from the overnight fall but were still down about 1.6% in Friday trading.

Reddit stock was down by 26%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.

Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by nearly 20%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.

Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.

Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.

He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".

"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

Gaming_Tech.title: How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
Gaming_Tech.text:
The moment she saw footage from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Kacey Doran picked up her phone. She had to tell her sister.

"Have you seen this?" messaged Doran, excitedly.

Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. Ocarina's fantasy-like story, and beautiful music, enthralled them both.

It was also the first game Doran ever completed. Now, countless memories rushed back to her as she devoured clips of the fully redesigned version, due to arrive on the Switch 2 later this year.

Doran's sister messaged back: "I'm not tearing up… YOU'RE tearing up."

This is the power of nostalgia – and a perfect example of how video games can trigger it. Doran now teaches an esports course at Rowan University in New Jersey. She says the original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, had a "magical" quality that she hopes to rediscover, and also share with her sister's children.

The video games industry has long leaned on remakes. From Mario Kart to the Final Fantasy series, or even Pac-Man, some games just keep coming back in updated forms, as new generations of gamers emerge and as computer hardware improves, enabling more detailed graphics and increasingly expansive game worlds.

While the emotional hook may be the most significant draw, putting out a remake can be a double-edged sword. Some gamers are very protective of their favourite titles and new versions don't always meet certain fans' astronomically high expectations.

Nostalgia is an important but mixed emotion, says Tim Wulf, at the Centre for Advanced Internet Studies in Bochum, Germany. It has positive aspects but also a kind of sadness, too. Happiness in remembering things that were important to us, and also an awareness that that time is now gone.

"It's a social emotion because memories that induce nostalgia for us are connected to other people," he explains, adding that nostalgia can boost our self-esteem while highlighting key social bonds.

Video games, says Wulf, are notoriously good at triggering nostalgia because gamers can "jump into the same environment". In other words, games are like time machines for our emotions, and returning to fondly remembered places can feel stabilising or reassuring in an ever-changing world.

Doran, for one, notes that when you return to a favourite old game, there's something satisfying about deploying previously learned skills. You know what to do here, you're winning again. Just like the old days.

Putting out remasters and remakes has been a "really successful" strategy for the games industry, says Piers Harding-Rolls, head of games research at Ampere Analysis.

"Tying in with established audiences and building on existing content is quite a safe route for a lot of companies," he adds. In many cases, it is cheaper to update an existing game rather than create a new title from scratch.

Among other remakes that have found big audiences recently are those of Resident Evil 4 and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.

But Ocarina of Time perhaps stands out because, ever since its original release, it has been considered by many as one of the greatest games ever made. "The interest from all the Gen Zs that I work with is really high," says Harding-Rolls. The legend of The Legend of Zelda, as it were.

Clearly, nostalgia is not the only driver of interest in the remake, and today's audiences will expect a game that plays to today's standards.

Games companies must keep innovating when linking contemporary audiences to the past, says Wulf, in order satisfy their desire for fresh experiences. And although Wulf himself was a big fan of the original, he has no personal interest in the Ocarina of Time remake. "I want a new game – I don't want to play an old game," he says. Nostalgia isn't always enough for some.

Plus, critics often highlight a tension between originals and remakes. Which is the definitive version? In 2021, Square Enix released the bizarrely titled Nier Replicant ver.1.22474487139... – a remaster of a game first published in 2010. One reviewer wrote, external, "What we're left with is two nearly identical Niers each vying to be the true Nier."

Fans may react badly should a remaster or remake fail to do justice to the source material. And, in the gaming world, angry fan reactions can be serious.

"There's always going to be that fan base or group of people that are going to nit-pick," says Stephanie Ijoma, chief executive and founder of NNESAGA, a consultancy and creative agency.

Ultimately, games developers working on remakes have to "find the right balance" between appealing to fans and allowing themselves to be creative with the material, she adds. "You can't make art in fear, you can't create in fear."

Ijoma gives the example of Final Fantasy VII. First released in 1997, it got a highly anticipated remake in 2020.

This was a game Ijoma played back in the late 1990s and she was thrilled to be able to share it with younger players today.

Remakes enable this sharing of experiences because getting old computer hardware or video games consoles to work, while a pastime loved by some, is not possible for everyone.

"I've tried multiple times to play Silent Hill 2 because I'm interested in older games but it's such a difficult game to come into nowadays," says Niklas Hallin, a solo indie game developer who runs the studio Neckbolt. "They made a remake and it's so smooth, it just works. It works on your modern hardware."

Hallin did not play many games as a child so he says nostalgia isn't much of a motivator for him. However, in his own games, he likes to include subtle stylistic references to classic games because he knows that this appeals to gamers.

Indie developers often lean on retro games aesthetics not just because people respond well to them – but also because they are easier to achieve. "You can't compete with billion dollar budgets, super high-fidelity, Triple A graphics," he says.

One question remains. The visual difference, today, between games released years apart is, arguably, negligible. So will there be any point in remaking a game from 2026 in, say, 2038? Will technology have moved on so much by then that it's actually worth it?

Harding-Rolls predicts that games companies will still seek to connect new audiences with classic titles by offering updates.

Remakes might become less about graphical improvements and more about editorial adjustments. "Reinterpretations," he says. "Or versions with additional content."

It's never really "game over", is it?

Gaming_Tech.title: Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
Gaming_Tech.text:
Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.

Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.

Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.

Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.

Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.

She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term.

"I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.

In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.

However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.

Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.

By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.

Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."

Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race.

But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.

Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours trading.

Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.

That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.

Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.

Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.

"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."

As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.

"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
